title: Sensory deficiencies in secondary neuropathies, psychiatric and psychosomatic disorders. A pediatric comparative study
summary:
Disturbed sensory perception is known for different pediatric conditions.  In patients with diabetes mellitus or chemotherapy because of malignancies it occurs as a secondary disease. Children with psychosomatic disorders experience disturbed perception despite the absence of an underlying somatic disorder, and children disturbed self-inflicted injuries also show altered sensory perception of so far unknown etiology. 
In contrast to nerve conductance studies which detect changes of large fiber function, quantitative sensory testing (QST) is able to detect a spectrum of sensory functions, including function of small intradermal nerve fibers. So far, only limited knowledge on this method is available for the pediatric population. 
In this study QST is used to study sensory perception in the above mentioned patient groups in comparison to healthy infants and children. The major questions are whether QST testing can detect disturbances in sensory perception in these patient groups, whether the patient groups differ with regard to distinct QST subtests and wether disturbances of sensory perception change over time in children with diabetes mellitus as well as with oncological diseases.

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
Age 5 - 17 years
Presence of diabetes mellitus, of an oncological disease prior to the initiation of therapy, of a psychosomatic pain disorder, of a psychiatric disorder with self-inflicted injury or normal child
Exclusion criteria:
For all probands: written consent not available.
for the normal probands: familial neuropathies. Medications that may influence sensory perception.
